BREAKING: Grok is helping @SpaceX inspect rocket parts. In a test for debris inside a tube, Grok scored 99.9%, compared with about 94% for human inspectors. 

Kiko Dontchev, SpaceX’s VP of Launch, shared a lot of new updates at UP Summit:

• SpaceX sees itself as an infrastructure company. It’s already building on Earth and in low Earth orbit, with the Moon next and Mars farther down the road.

• AI adoption took off at SpaceX this year. Dontchev says it’s the biggest jump in engineering speed he’s seen in 16 years at the company. Some tasks that took hours or days now take seconds or minutes.

• Grok is checking rocket hardware for debris. In one example, human inspectors spotted debris inside tubes about 94% of the time. Grok reached 99.9% on the same inspection footage.

• SpaceX has also automated visual checks on Starlink dishes. Technicians and team leads now use AI in their daily work, and Dontchev says it’s helping people build skills faster.

• Settling Mars remains a core SpaceX goal. Dontchev believes AI can help the company get to both the Moon and Mars faster.

• Falcon 9 still needs a fresh upper stage every flight. That works at around 100 launches a year. To reach thousands of launches a year, potentially even 10,000 someday, SpaceX wants to catch and reuse both stages of Starship.

• Starship’s first orbital flight in September deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Together, they represented about 10× the network capacity of a typical Falcon 9 Starlink launch.

• From Florida, a single Starship launch could put up to 20× the Starlink capacity of a Falcon 9 launch into orbit. Florida offers a more direct path to some orbits, saving fuel and letting Starship carry more satellites.

• Starship’s launch pad at Kennedy Space Center’s Pad 39A is nearly ready. SpaceX hopes to send the first boosters and ships from Texas by barge in December. The first Florida launch could happen before the end of 2026.
